Electrical Fundamentals
 Electric Motor Insulation Classes: Class A, B, F and H Explained
 Motor insulation class defines the maximum temperature the winding insulation can withstand without degrading. Choosing the wrong class shortens motor life. Understanding it helps you specify, select, and protect motors correctly.
 Class A: 105°C 
 Class B: 130°C 
 Class F: 155°C 
 Class H: 180°C 
 Temperature Rise 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn about electric motor insulation classes . We will understand the four standard classes (A, B, F, H), what the temperature limits mean, how to calculate the allowable temperature rise, and how to choose the right class for your motor application.
 Every motor nameplate carries an insulation class letter that tells you the maximum temperature the winding can survive.
 Running above this limit causes exponential insulation degradation. The 10-degree rule states that every 10°C above the rated limit halves the insulation life.
 Quick Answer
 What Are the Insulation Classes of a Motor?
 Motor insulation class is the letter on the nameplate that sets the maximum winding temperature the insulation can withstand. The four standard classes are A, B, F and H.

 Temperature Budget: How Class, Rise and Margin Add Up
 The insulation class limit is built from three components: ambient temperature + allowable temperature rise + hot-spot allowance. Understanding this budget shows how much thermal margin is left for overloads.
 Did You Know? The 10-degree rule for insulation life means that every 10°C above the rated class limit halves the insulation's expected service life. A Class F motor (rated to 155°C) running continuously at 165°C will have half the expected winding life. At 175°C it will have one-quarter the life. This is why even small, sustained overloads are disproportionately damaging to motor insulation, and why the thermal overload relay is the most important motor protection device.

 Right vs Wrong Insulation Class Selection
 Correct Selection
 Class F or H for VFD-driven motors (harmonic heating)
 Class H when ambient exceeds 40°C
 Class H for intermittent duty or frequent starts
 Class F minimum for all new industrial installations
 Insulation class checked against actual measured winding temperature
 Common Mistakes
 Class B motor used on VFD (harmonic losses push winding above 130°C)
 Class A or B in high-ambient enclosures (ambient alone may exceed rise budget)
 Assuming Class F nameplate rating means the motor runs at 155°C (it runs cooler)
 Ignoring service factor SF 1.15 means motor can run at 115% load, not 115% temperature
 Using Class B motor as direct replacement for failed Class F without checking thermal margin
 Tip: Using a Class F motor with Class B temperature rise gives a 25°C thermal margin. 
Many modern motors are designed with Class F insulation but specified to run with Class B temperature rise (80°C rise at 40°C ambient). This means the winding only reaches 120°C in normal operation, but the insulation is rated to 155°C. The 35°C margin extends motor life significantly and handles overloads, high ambient, or harmonic heating without risk. This practice is called Class F insulation with Class B rise.

 Motor Insulation Class Questions Engineers Ask
 What is motor insulation class?
 Motor insulation class defines the maximum continuous temperature the winding insulation can withstand without significant degradation. The four standard classes are A (105°C), B (130°C), F (155°C), and H (180°C).
 What is the most common motor insulation class in industrial use?
 Class F (155°C) is the most common insulation class in modern industrial motors. Many Class F motors run at Class B temperature rise, giving extra thermal margin at lower cost.
 What is the difference between insulation class and temperature rise?
 Insulation class is the maximum winding temperature. Temperature rise is the difference between winding temperature and ambient temperature. At 40°C ambient, Class F allows a 105°C rise to reach 155°C.
 Why is Class H insulation used for VFD-driven motors?
 VFD output harmonics cause additional losses in the stator winding, raising the winding temperature above what the fundamental current alone would produce. Class H insulation provides the extra thermal margin needed.
 What is the 10-degree rule for motor insulation?
 The 10-degree rule states that every 10°C above the insulation class limit halves the expected insulation life. A motor running 20°C above its limit has only one-quarter of its rated service life.

 What We Learn Today
 Four standard motor insulation classes exist: A (105°C), B (130°C), F (155°C), and H (180°C). The temperature limit is the sum of ambient temperature, allowable rise, and hot-spot allowance. Class F with Class B rise is the most common practice in modern industrial motors.
 The 10-degree rule: every 10°C above the insulation class limit halves the winding service life. A motor running 20°C over its class limit has only one-quarter of its rated insulation life.
 Use Class H insulation for VFD-driven motors, motors in ambient temperatures above 40°C, and motors with frequent starts or intermittent duty cycles. Class F is the minimum for all new industrial motor installations.

 F Class Insulation Temperature: 155°C Limit and Life Margin
 F class insulation temperature is 155°C, the maximum hot spot temperature the winding insulation can withstand for its normal design life. At the standard 40°C ambient this allows a temperature rise of 105°C plus a 10°C hot spot allowance, which adds up to 155°C.
 Many industrial motors use Class F insulation but are designed so the winding only rises as much as a Class B motor, about 80°C. The hot spot then sits near 40 + 80 + 10 = 130°C, leaving about 25°C of thermal reserve for overloads, high ambient or VFD heating.

 How to check a Class F motor
 Read the insulation class and ambient rating on the nameplate.
 Measure the winding temperature, for example by resistance or embedded detectors.
 Subtract the ambient to get the actual rise and compare it with 105°C.
 Keep the hot spot below 155°C; every 10°C above it halves the life.
 This is why small sustained overloads do more damage than they seem to, and why correct overload relay settings matter.
